subject: music
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: To which family of the orchestra does the oboe belong?
questions.explain: The oboe is a woodwind instrument, played using a double reed.

questions.q: Which is the lowest-pitched member of the orchestral string family?
questions.explain: The double bass is the largest and lowest-sounding of the standard orchestral strings.

questions.q: How is sound produced on a brass instrument such as the trumpet?
options: By the player buzzing their lips into a mouthpiece
questions.explain: Brass players create sound by vibrating (buzzing) their lips against a cup-shaped mouthpiece.

questions.q: Which of these woodwind instruments uses a double reed?
questions.explain: The bassoon (like the oboe) sounds through a double reed, whereas the clarinet uses a single reed and the flute has no reed.

questions.q: Which of the following is a pitched (tuned) percussion instrument?
questions.explain: The xylophone plays definite pitches, making it tuned percussion, unlike the snare drum, triangle or cymbals.

questions.q: In what way does a clarinet differ from an oboe?
options: The clarinet uses a single reed
The clarinet is a brass instrument
The clarinet is played with a bow
questions.explain: The clarinet produces its sound with a single reed, while the oboe uses a double reed.

questions.q: The instruction 'pizzicato' tells a string player to do what?
options: Pluck the strings with the fingers
questions.explain: 'Pizzicato' means to pluck the strings rather than bow them (arco).

questions.q: Which grouping correctly names the four instrumental families of the orchestra?
questions.explain: The orchestra is traditionally divided into the strings, woodwind, brass and percussion families.

questions.q: What is the defining feature of an ensemble performance?
options: Two or more performers playing together
A performance played entirely from memory
questions.explain: An ensemble performance involves two or more musicians performing together.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a solo and an ensemble performance?
options: In an ensemble the performer must play from memory
In an ensemble two or more musicians perform together and must coordinate
A solo must always be sung rather than played
A solo cannot use any accompaniment at all
questions.explain: A solo is performed by one player, whereas an ensemble needs two or more performers working together.

questions.q: Why does playing a melody over a pre-recorded backing track on its own not count as a genuine ensemble part?
options: Backing tracks are always too loud
An ensemble requires the candidate to combine with at least one other live performer
Solo playing is not allowed in the GCSE
Backing tracks change the key automatically
questions.explain: A true ensemble part interacts with at least one other live musician's independent part, not just a fixed backing.

questions.q: A student plays a duet with another musician, listening carefully and adjusting to stay together. This is best described as:
questions.explain: Performing interdependently with another live musician is ensemble performance.

questions.q: In a performance, what does good 'intonation' mean?
questions.explain: Intonation refers to the accuracy of pitch, i.e. playing in tune.

questions.q: What do 'dynamics' refer to in a performance?
options: The loudness and softness of the music
questions.explain: Dynamics describe how loud or soft the music is played.

questions.q: Which of these best demonstrates good 'ensemble' skill?
options: Keeping together with the other performers, listening and balancing well
Playing as loudly as possible throughout
Ignoring the other players to focus on your own part
Choosing the most difficult piece available
questions.explain: Good ensemble skill means listening, staying together and balancing your part with the others.

questions.q: During a piece a performer keeps rushing ahead of the beat. Which performance skill most needs improvement?
options: Maintaining a steady tempo and pulse
questions.explain: Rushing ahead of the beat is a problem of keeping a steady tempo and secure sense of pulse.

questions.q: What does 'articulation' describe in a performance?
options: How individual notes are attacked and shaped, such as legato or staccato
How loud the music is overall
The key the piece is played in
questions.explain: Articulation is the way notes are begun and joined, for example smoothly (legato) or detached (staccato).

questions.q: In an ensemble, the pianist plays so loudly that the flute cannot be heard. This is a problem with:
questions.explain: When one part drowns out another, the ensemble's balance is at fault.

questions.q: A composer wants a warm, deep, low sustained sound from the brass family. Which instrument is the best choice?
questions.explain: The tuba is the lowest brass instrument, ideal for warm, deep sustained bass sounds.

questions.q: Choosing suitable tempo, dynamics and phrasing to express the character of a piece is known as:
questions.explain: Interpretation is the performer's shaping of tempo, dynamics and phrasing to convey the character of the music.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) Music (J536) specification; Area of Study 1: My Music (Performance)
